# Introduction {#sec-intro}

In many empirical
applications, researchers
employ multiple instrumental
variables in \textbf{two-stage
least squares} (\textbf{2SLS})
estimation in order to improve
statistical efficiency. When
treatment effects are
constant, combining several
valid instruments strengthens
the first stage, reduces
sampling variance, and leads
to more precise estimates. In
such settings, the use of
multiple instruments is
uncontroversial and often
desirable, and efficiency
considerations alone provide a
compelling justification for
their use.

The standard causal
interpretation of 2SLS is
rooted in the Local Average
Treatment Effect (LATE)
framework of @imbens1994. With
a single binary instrument
alongside a standard
monotonicity assumption, 2SLS
identifies the average
treatment effect for those
individuals whose treatment
status is changed by the
instrument, this kind of
individuals are known as the
\textbf{compliers}. This
interpretation has become a
cornerstone of modern
empirical practice. When
multiple instruments are
available, @angrist1995 showed
that the 2SLS estimand can be
interpreted as a positively
weighted average of local
average treatment effects
(LATEs) for subpopulations
whose treatment status is
affected by the instruments.

However, justifying this
interpretation in the
multiple-instrument setting
requires a strong
generalization of the standard
monotonicity assumption. As
shown by @mogstad2021, this
assumption is extremely
restrictive and is frequently
violated once treatment
effects are heterogeneous.
Importantly, the problem does
not arise from high
dimensionality or technical
complexity. Instead, it is
inherent to the use of more
than one instrument, even in
the simplest possible
environments.

To make this point
transparent, this paper
focuses on the simplest
nontrivial setting: a binary
treatment and two binary
instrumental variables. Even
in this minimal environment,
the standard monotonicity
assumption, which will be
called "Imbens and Angrist
monotonicity", or
\textbf{IAM}, imposes strong
restrictions on individual
treatment choice behavior.
With four possible instrument
states, the assumption
requires that each
individual’s treatment
decisions across these states
can be ordered in a single,
consistent direction. As a
result, individuals cannot
respond to different
instruments in meaningfully
different ways.

This restriction is difficult
to reconcile with applied
work. In empirical practice,
different instruments
typically represent distinct
sources of exogenous
variation, such as
institutional rules, policy
thresholds, or geographic
constraints. It is therefore
natural to expect that
different instruments affect
different individuals and move
different margins of the
population into treatment.
Nevertheless, such instruments
are often combined in a single
2SLS regression and
interpreted as if they were
reinforcing the same causal
effect. The key insight of
@mogstad2021 is that IAM does
much more than rule out
defiers: in the presence of
multiple instruments, it
effectively rules out
economically meaningful
heterogeneity in how different
instruments affect treatment.

The main contribution of the
paper is to make this
restriction explicit and to
propose a more credible
alternative. The authors
introduce \textbf{partial
monotonicity}, which requires
that each instrument, holding
the other instruments fixed,
affects treatment in a weakly
monotone way. This weaker
assumption allows different
instruments to influence
different subpopulations,
while still ruling out
perverse responses to each
instrument individually.

Under partial monotonicity,
2SLS continues to admit a
causal interpretation, but its
nature changes in an important
way. Rather than identifying a
single local average treatment
effect, the 2SLS estimand
becomes a weighted average of
multiple group-specific causal
effects, and these weights do
not need to be all positive.
The paper provides a complete
characterization of this
estimand, clarifies the
economic meaning of the
resulting weights, and shows
how their signs are directly
linked to observable
first-stage relationships.

The remainder of this term
paper proceeds as follows.
Section 2 will provide a
detailed overview of Mogstad,
Torgovitsky, and Walters'
methodology and framework,
introduces IAM and partial
monotonicity assumptions, and
discusses their implications
for treatment choice behavior.
Section 5 examines the
empirical implications of the
framework and illustrates the
results using a simulation.
Section 6 discusses
limitations, open questions,
and potential extensions, and
concludes.

## Literature Review

The starting point for the
present paper is the classic
LATE interpretation of IV
under heterogeneity.
@imbens1994 established that
with a single binary
instrument and monotonicity,
IV identifies a complier
average causal effect.
@angrist1995 then extended
this logic to multiple
instruments, showing that 2SLS
can be interpreted as a
positively weighted average of
instrument-specific LATEs
under a multi-instrument
monotonicity condition. The
contribution of the present
paper is best understood as a
sharp critique of how
restrictive this
multi-instrument monotonicity
requirement becomes.

Related work by the same
authors develops complementary
implications of weakening
global monotonicity.
@mogstad2024 can be read as a
direct extension of the
present paper’s perspective
from the interpretation of the
linear 2SLS estimand to the
identification of broader
policy-relevant objects. While
the present paper
characterizes what 2SLS means
under partial monotonicity,
@mogstad2024 uses the same
partial monotonicity
restriction to extract and
aggregate information from
multiple instruments for
target parameters beyond 2SLS.
In this sense, it extends the
present paper’s core message,
that interpretation depends on
behavioral restrictions, into
a framework aimed at policy
evaluation rather than linear
estimation.

Subsequent work has also taken
the present paper’s
assumptions as objects of
empirical scrutiny. @jiang2023
addresses a practical
implication of the present
paper: once one replaces the
strong global monotonicity
requirement with partial
monotonicity, a natural
question is whether partial
monotonicity is plausible in
applications. The paper
responds by proposing a simple
nonparametric test for partial
monotonicity, assessing its
finite-sample behavior in
simulations, and illustrating
it in an empirical
application.

A related, more structural
refinement is provided by
@goff2024. This paper shares
the present @mogstad2021
motivation, in that global
multi-instrument monotonicity
is often too restrictive, but
proposes a different
weakening, vector
monotonicity, which requires
treatment uptake to be
monotone in each instrument
without imposing a global
ordering when instruments
shift in opposing directions.
Relative to the present paper,
its contribution is to
characterize which causal
parameters become point
identified under this
alternative restriction and to
provide constructive
estimation results.
Conceptually, it highlights
that once global monotonicity
is relaxed, different
monotonicity notions lead to
different identifiable
objects, reinforcing the
present paper’s central
emphasis on interpretability
rather than mechanical
estimation.

# Methodology Overview

Following the motivation
outlined in @sec-intro, this
second chapter contains the
methodology developed by
@mogstad2021.

## Framework and Assumptions

### Setup and Potential Outcomes

To fix ideas and keep the
exposition transparent, this
section focuses on the
simplest nontrivial setting
considered in the paper: a
\textbf{binary treatment} and
\textbf{two binary instrumental variables}.
While the theoretical results
extend to more general
environments, the central
insights already arise in this
minimal framework.

Let $D_i \in \{0,1\}$ denote a
binary treatment and $Y_i$ the
observed outcome for
individual $i$. Each
individual is characterized by
potential outcomes $Y_i(1)$
and $Y_i(0)$, corresponding to
the potential outcomes under
treatment and control,
respectively. The observed
outcome can thus be expressed
as: \begin{equation}
Y_i = D_i Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i) Y_i(0).
\end{equation}

Treatment assignment depends
on two binary instruments,
\begin{equation}
Z_i = (Z_{i1}, Z_{i2}) \in \{0,1\}^2,
\end{equation} which generate
four possible instrument
realizations: $(0,0)$,
$(0,1)$, $(1,0)$, and $(1,1)$.
Treatment choice is described
by a potential treatment
function $D_i(z_1, z_2)$,
allowing for heterogeneous
responses across individuals
and differential responses to
the two instruments.

### 2SLS Estimand

The object of interest is the
two-stage least squares
estimand, denoted
$\beta_{2SLS}$. The population
2SLS estimand can be written
as \begin{equation}
\beta_{2SLS} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\tilde{D}_i\tilde{Y}_i]}{\mathbb{E}[\tilde{D}_i^2]},
\end{equation} where
$\tilde{D}_i = \mathbb{E}[D_i|Z_i] - \mathbb{E}[D_i]$
and
$\tilde{Y}_i = \mathbb{e}[Y_i|Z_i] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i]$
denote the residualized
treatment and outcome with
respect to the instrument
space. Equivalently,
$\beta_{2SLS}$ can be
expressed as \begin{equation}
\beta_{2SLS} = \frac{\text{Cov}(\mathbb{E}[D_i|Z_i], \mathbb{E}[Y_i|Z_i]),}{\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[D_i|Z_i])}.
\end{equation} In the
binary-instrument setting,
this representation highlights
that the 2SLS estimand
aggregates outcome differences
across instrument-induced
changes in treatment
propensity. Under standard
instrumental variables
assumptions, this estimand is
well defined and consistently
estimated by sample 2SLS.

The focus of the present paper
is not on estimation or
consistency, but on the causal
interpretation of
$\beta_{2SLS}$. In particular,
the central question is, under
which assumptions on treatment
choice behavior can
$\beta_{2SLS}$ be written as a
weighted average of causal
effects, and which causal
effects are being aggregated?
Addressing this question
requires explicit assumptions
on how the instruments affect
treatment.

## Imbens and Angrist Monotonicity (IAM)

A natural starting point is
the extension of the standard
monotonicity assumption from
the single-instrument LATE
framework, known as Imbens and
Angrist Monotonicity (IAM).

\textbf{Definition 1 (Imbens and Angrist Monotonicity)}

\textit{For all $z, z' \in \mathcal{Z}$ either $D_i(z) \ge D_i(z')$ for all $i \in \mathcal{I}$, or $D_i(z) \le D_i(z')$ for all $i \in \mathcal{I}$.}

Under IAM, there must exist a
global ordering of the four
instrument values such that,
for every individual,
treatment status moves weakly
in the same direction along
this ordering.

When IAM holds, the 2SLS
estimand admits a causal
interpretation as a weighted
average of local average
treatment effects.
Importantly, IAM is not an
assumption imposed separately
on each instrument. Rather, it
is a joint restriction across
all instrument combinations.

While this monotonicity
assumption in the
single-instrument case simply
rules out defiers and is often
viewed as a mild behavioral
restriction, IAM becomes
substantially more demanding
when multiple instruments are
present. In particular, it
places strong constraints on
heterogeneity in treatment
choice by requiring all
instruments to operate along
the same margin of
individuals.

## Partial Monotonicity

To address the restrictiveness
of IAM, the paper proposes a
weaker alternative called
partial monotonicity.

\textbf{Definition 2 (Partial Monotonicity)}

\textit{Take any $l = 1, \dots, L$, and let $(z_l, z_{-l})$ and $(z'_l, z_{-l})$ be two points in $\mathcal{Z}$. Then, either $D_i(z_l, z_{-l}) \ge D_i(z'_l, z_{-l})$ for all $i \in \mathcal{I}$, or or $D_i(z_l, z_{-l}) \le D_i(z'_l, z_{-l})$ for all $i \in \mathcal{I}$.}

Partial monotonicity relaxes
the global ordering
requirement imposed by IAM
while retaining enough
structure to support causal
interpretation.

Formally, partial monotonicity
requires that each instrument
affects treatment in a weakly
monotone way when
\textbf{holding the other instrument fixed}.
That is, increasing $Z_{i1}$
from 0 to 1 cannot induce some
individuals to enter treatment
and others to exit treatment
conditional on $Z_{i2}$, and
analogously for $Z_{i2}$.

Crucially, partial
monotonicity does not impose a
global ordering across all
instrument combinations. As a
result, it allows exactly the
type of heterogeneity that IAM
rules out. Different
instruments may affect
different subpopulations, one
instrument may induce
treatment for one group of
individuals, while the other
operates on a distinct margin.
From an economic perspective,
this behavior is often natural
when instruments capture
different incentives or
constraints.

### Response Groups under Partial Monotonicity

The partial monotonicity
assumption implies that
individuals can be classified
into distinct response groups
based on how their treatment
status responds to changes in
each instrument. In the
binary-instrument setting, we
have \begin{equation}
Z_i = (Z_{i1}, Z_{i2}) \in \{0,1\}^2,
\end{equation} which generate
four possible instrument
values
$z_1 = (0,0), z_2 = (0,1), z_3 = (1,0), z_4 = (1,1)$.
Treatment choice is described
by the potential treatment
function $D_i(z_1,z_2)$, which
specifies whether individual
$i$ receives treatment under
each instrument realization.

The following proposition,
establishes that the
population can be partitioned
into six exclusive response
groups.

\textbf{Proposition 1}[^1]:

[^1]: This proposition is
    adapted from @mogstad2021.

\textit{If $\mathcal{Z} = \{0,1\}^2$ and partial monotonicity holds with the following order:}
\begin{equation}
D_i(0,0) \le D_i(0,1) \le D_i(1,1),
\end{equation} \textit{and}
\begin{equation}
D_i(0,0) \le D_i(1,0) \le D_i(1,1),
\end{equation}
\textit{then each $i \in \mathcal{I}$ belongs exactly to one of the six groups in Table 1.}

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{c c c c c}
\hline
\textbf{Group} $G_i$ & $D_i(0,0)$ & $D_i(0,1)$
 & $D_i(1,0)$ & $D_i(1,1)$ \\
\hline
Always-taker (\textbf{at}) & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
Eager complier (\textbf{ec}) & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
Reluctant complier (\textbf{rc}) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
Never-taker (\textbf{nt}) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
$Z_1$ complier (\textbf{c1}) & 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\
$Z_2$ complier (\textbf{c2}) & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{Response Groups under Partial Monotonicity}
\end{table}

Since the focus is on the
causal interpretation of 2SLS,
four of these six groups are
particularly relevant:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{$Z_1$ compliers (c1)}: individuals whose treatment status changes when $Z_{i1}$ switches from 0 to 1, holding $Z_{i2}$ fixed, but who do not respond to changes in $Z_{i2}$.
\item \textbf{$Z_2$ compliers (c2)}: individuals whose treatment status changes when $Z_{i2}$ switches from 0 to 1, holding $Z_{i1}$ fixed, but who do not respond to changes in $Z_{i1}$.
\item \textbf{Eager compliers (ec)}: individuals who enter treatment when either instrument is activated. For these individuals, both instruments independently push them into treatment.
\item \textbf{Reluctant compliers (rc)}: individuals who enter treatment only when both instruments are active. Each instrument alone is insufficient, but their joint activation induces treatment.
\end{enumerate}

These groups generalize the
familiar complier concept from
the single-instrument LATE
framework and reflect the fact
that different instruments may
operate on different margins
of the population. In
particular, individuals are
allowed to respond differently
to different instruments, as
long as each instrument moves
treatment in a consistent
direction holding the other
fixed.

## 2SLS Estimand under Partial Monotonicity

### Instrumental Variable Assumptions

The 2SLS estimand under
partial monotonicity is
derived naturally under
partial monotonicity, but also
under the standard
instrumental-variables
assumptions.

\textbf{Instrument Relevance:} \textit{Each instrument has a nonzero effect on the probability of treatment:}
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}(D_i = 1 | Z_{i,l} = 1) \ne \mathbb{P}(D_i = 1 | Z_{i,l} = 0), \quad l \in \{1,2\}.
\end{equation}
\textbf{Instrument Exogeneity:} \textit{The instruments are independent of potential outcomes and potential treatments:}
\begin{equation}
(Y_i(0), Y_i(1), \{D_i(z)\}_{z \in \mathcal{Z}}) \perp Z_i.
\end{equation}
\textbf{Exclusion:} \textit{Instruments affect the outcome only through treatment:}
\begin{equation}
Y_i(z) = Y_i(D_i(z)) \quad \textit{for all } z \in \mathcal{Z}.
\end{equation}

### Causal Interpretation of 2SLS under Partial Monotonicity

\textbf{Theorem 1}[^2]:

[^2]: This theorem is adapted
    from @mogstad2021.

\textit{Suppose the instrument vector $Z_i = (Z_{i1}, Z_{i2})$ has support $\mathcal{Z} = \{0,1\}^2$, and that \textbf{partial monotonicity, instrument relevance, instrument exogeneity, and the exclusion restriction} hold. Suppose further that the potential outcomes are well-defined and that the 2SLS estimand $\beta_{2SLS}$ exists. Then, the 2SLS estimand can be expressed as:}
\begin{equation}
\beta_{2SLS} = \sum_{g \in \{1c, 2c, ec, rc\}} w_g \Delta_g,
\end{equation}
\textit{where $\Delta_g$ denotes the average treatment effect for response group $g$, and $w_g$ are weights with $\sum_g w_g = 1$. Both the weights of eager compliers and reluctant compliers are always nonnegative, i.e. $w_{ec}, w_{rc} \ge 0$, while one of the weights of $Z_1$ compliers or $Z_2$ compliers can be negative.}

\textit{If $\pi_{1c} \ge \pi_{2c}$ where $\pi_g := \mathbb{P}(G_i = g)$, then $w_{1c}$ is also nonnegative, while the sign of $w_{2c}$ is given by:}
\begin{equation}
\text{sgn}(w_{2c}) = \mathbb{I}[\pi_{2c} > 0] \times \text{sgn}[\mathbb{P}(D_i = 1 | Z_{i,2} = 1] - \mathbb{P}[D_i = 1 | Z_{i,2} = 0)].
\end{equation}
\textit{If $\pi_{2c} \ge \pi_{1c}$, then $w_{2c}$ is nonnegative, while the sign of $w_{1c}$ is given by}
\begin{equation}
\text{sgn}(w_{1c}) = \mathbb{I}[\pi_{1c} > 0] \times \text{sgn}[\mathbb{P}(D_i = 1 | Z_{i,1} = 1) - \mathbb{P}(D_i = 1 | Z_{i,1} = 0)].
\end{equation}

This theorem establishes that the 2SLS estimand can be interpreted as a weighted average of average treatment effects for the four possible groups that change treatment status in response to the one or both of the instruments.

The economic intuition is that some changes in the instrument values, specifically the shift from $(0,1)$ to $(1,0)$ can generate two-way treatment flows, this means that one group of individuals enters treatment while another exits. When this happens, the associated complier group receives a negative weight.

This result provides a complete characterization of what 2SLS identifies under partial monotonicity. Rather than a single LATE, the estimand aggregates causal effects across multiple response groups, with the sign and magnitude of the weights determined by observable first-stage relationships.

\textbf{Proof of Theorem 1}[^3]:

[^3]: This proof is also adapted
    from @mogstad2021.
    
The goal of the proof is to show that, under partial monotonicity and standard IV assumptions, the 2SLS estimand can be expressed as a weighted average of group-specific treatment effects, and to characterize precisely when one of these weights may be negative.

The proof begins by labeling the four possible realizations of the two binary instruments as
\begin{equation}
z^1 = (0,0), z^2 = (0,1), z^3 = (1,0), z^4 = (1,1),
\end{equation} and denoting their probabilites as $q_k = \mathbb{P}(Z_i = z^k)$ for $k = 1, \dots, 4$. Let
\begin{equation}
p_k = \mathbb{P}[D_i = 1 | Z_i = z^k],
\end{equation} denote the propensity score associated with instrument value $z^k$. Under partial monotonicity and the ordering assumed in the paper, these propensity scores are weakly increasing in $k$. A key result used in the proof is a result due to Angrist and Imbens, which shows that in this setting the 2SLS estimand can be written as a convex combination of three Wald estimands corresponding to adjacent changes in the instrument values, i.e.
\begin{equation}
\beta_{2SLS} = \lambda_2 w_2 + \lambda_3 w_3 + \lambda_4 w_4,
\end{equation} where the coefficients $\lambda_k$ are positive weights and sum to one. The Wald estimands $w_k$ are defined as
\begin{equation}
w_k := \frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i | Z_i = z^k] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i | Z_i = z^{k-1}]}{p(z^k) - p(z^{k-1})}, \quad k = 2,3,4.
\end{equation} Each Wald estimand captures the average causal effect for individuals whose treatment status changes when the instrument moves from $z^{k-1}$ to $z^k$. The weights $\lambda_k$ are defined as
\begin{equation}
\lambda_k := \frac{(p(z^k) - p(z^{k-1}))\sum_{l=k}^4 q^l(p(z^l) - \mathbb{E}[p(Z_i)])}{\sum_{j=2}^4 [(p(z^j) - p(z^{j-1})) \sum_{l=j}^4 q^l (p(z^l) - \mathbb{E}[p(Z_i)])]}.
\end{equation} The group definitions from Proposition 1 implies that $w_2$ represents the average treatment effect for both the $Z_2$ compliers and the eager compliers. Similarly, $w_4$ captures the average treatment effect for $Z_2$ compliers and reluctant compliers, i.e.
\begin{equation}
w_2 = \left(\frac{\pi_{2c}}{\pi_{2c} + \pi_{ec}}\right)\Delta_{2c} + \left(\frac{\pi_{ec}}{\pi_{2c} + \pi_{ec}}\right)\Delta_{ec}
\end{equation} and
\begin{equation}
w_4 = \left(\frac{\pi_{2c}}{\pi_{2c} + \pi_{rc}}\right)\Delta_{2c} + \left(\frac{\pi_{rc}}{\pi_{2c} + \pi_{rc}}\right)\Delta_{rc}.
\end{equation} For the transitions from $z^1 \rightarrow z^2$ and from $z^3 \rightarrow z^4$, only one instrument changes while the other is held fixed. Under partial monotonicity, these transitions induce one-directional treatment movements, i.e. individuals either enter treatment or remain untreated. As a result, the corresponding Wald estimands can be written as weighted averages of treatment effects for well-defined complier groups. Importantly, all weights involved in these decompositions are nonnegative.

However, the crucial part comes from the transition from $z^2 = (0,1) \rightarrow z^3 = (1,0)$, which is different. Along this margin, one instrument increases while the other decreases. Partial monotonicity allows this change to generate \textbf{two-way treatment flows}, where $Z_1$ compliers enter treatment while $Z_2$ compliers exit treatment. Consequently, the Wald estimand $w_3$ can be expressed as
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
w_3 &= \frac{\mathbb{E}[(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0))(D_i(1,0) - D_i(0,1))]}{p(z^3) - p(z^2)}\\ &= \left(\frac{\pi_{1c}}{p(z^3) - p(z^2)}\right)\Delta_{1c} + \left(\frac{\pi_{2c}}{p(z^3) - p(z^2)} \right)\Delta_{2c} \\ &= \left(\frac{\pi_{1c}}{\pi_{1c} - \pi_{2c}}\right)\Delta_{1c} + \left(\frac{\pi_{2c}}{\pi_{1c} - \pi_{2c}} \right)\Delta_{2c}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation} Substituting the decompositions of the three Wald estimands back into the convex combination for $\beta_{2SLS}$ yields
\begin{equation}
\beta_{2SLS} = \sum_{g \in \{1c, 2c, ec, rc\}} w_g \Delta_g,
\end{equation} where
$$
\begin{aligned}
w_{ec} &:= \frac{\lambda_{2}\pi_{ec}}{\pi_{ec} + \pi_{2c}}, \\
w_{1c} &:= \frac{\lambda_3 \pi_{1c}}{\pi_{1c} - \pi_{2c}}, \\
w_{rc} &:= \frac{\lambda_4 \pi_{rc}}{\pi_{rc} + \pi_{2c}}, \\
w_{2c} &:= 
\left(\frac{\lambda_{2}\pi_{2c}}{\pi_{ec} + \pi_{2c}}\right)
- \left(\frac{\lambda_3\pi_{2c}}{\pi_{1c} - \pi_{2c}}\right)
+ \left(\frac{\lambda_4 \pi_{2c}}{\pi_{rc} + \pi_{2c}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ 
The proof shows that the weights on eager and reluctant compliers are always nonnegative, and that at most one instrument-specific complier group can receive a negative weight. Moreover, the sign of this potentially negative weight is not arbitrary, it is entirely determined by an observable first-stage object, specifically by the covariance between treatment and the corresponding instrument. In particular, the weight on $Z_2$ compliers is negative if and only if the first-stage effect of $Z_2$ on treatment is negative along the relevant margin.

The central insight of the proof is therefore that negative weights arise only when an instrument change induces offsetting treatment flows, i.e. some individuals enter treatment while others exit. Apart from this specific case, all components of the 2SLS estimand receive nonnegative weight.
